title: Security Misconfiguration & Logging Failures
summary: Most breaches don't need a clever exploit — a default password, a verbose error page, or a blind spot in your logs does the job. This topic covers the failures of absence and visibility that let small mistakes become full compromises.

slides.markdown:
Two of the ten [OWASP Top 10](owasp-top-10) categories — Security Misconfiguration and Security Logging & Monitoring Failures — aren't about a clever exploit technique at all. They're about **absence**: a setting left at its default, a feature left enabled that should be off, or a breach that ran for months because nobody was watching.

That makes them different to reason about than injection or XSS. There's no payload to craft. The fix is almost always "turn something off," "change a default," or "look at the logs you already have." And that's exactly why they're so common — they don't require an attacker to find a bug, only for a team to skip a step.

This topic covers both: the defaults and disclosures that hand an attacker a foothold, and the visibility gaps that let them keep it.

Security misconfiguration covers any gap between how a system *could* be secured and how it's actually deployed. The recurring patterns:

- **Default credentials** left unchanged — admin/admin on a database console, a default API key shipped in a starter template that goes straight to production.
- **Verbose stack traces** in error responses, which hand an attacker your framework version, file paths, and sometimes a snippet of the query that failed.
- **Open admin panels** reachable from the public internet with no network-level restriction, relying on the login page alone as the only gate.
- **Unnecessary features enabled** — directory listing on a web server, a debug console left reachable, sample apps shipped with the framework.
- **Permissive CORS** (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` combined with credentials) that lets any site read authenticated responses.

Each of these individually looks minor. Combined, they're how a single exposed admin console with a default password becomes a full data breach in one weekend, with no code vulnerability involved at all.

The single principle behind most misconfiguration fixes: **every enabled feature is attack surface, whether or not you use it.**

Concretely:

- A framework's debug mode should never reach production — it exists to help *you*, and it helps an attacker identically well.
- An unused HTTP method (`TRACE`, `OPTIONS` beyond what CORS needs) or an unused API version should be disabled, not left "just in case."
- Cloud resources — storage buckets, database instances — should be provisioned private by default and opened up deliberately, never the reverse.
- Sample applications and default pages that ship with a framework (a default `/admin` login, a `/phpinfo`-style diagnostics page) get deleted, not left "because nobody will find it." Attackers scan for exactly these paths at scale, automatically, within minutes of a host going live.

This is why hardening guides read like subtraction lists: turn off, remove, restrict. Security misconfiguration is rarely fixed by adding code — it's fixed by shrinking what's exposed.

slides.sectionTitle: What good security logging looks like
slides.markdown:
Logging and monitoring failures mean a breach happens and nobody notices — industry breach reports have repeatedly found median detection times measured in months, often via a third party or the attacker themselves (a ransom note), not the victim's own systems.

Good security logging captures, at minimum:

- **Authentication events** — every login success and failure, with enough context (IP, user agent, timestamp) to spot a credential-stuffing pattern.
- **Access control decisions** — especially denials. A spike in 403s against `/admin/*` from one IP is a reconnaissance signal.
- **High-value actions** — password changes, permission grants, data exports, admin actions — anything that changes who can do what or who can see what.
- **Input validation failures** — repeated malformed input against the same endpoint often precedes an injection attempt.

Just as important as capturing events is **alerting on them**. A log line nobody reads is only useful after the fact, in a forensic investigation — which is real value, but it's not detection. Detection needs a threshold and an on-call human or automated response on the other end.

Logging exists to detect abuse, but a log that captures the wrong fields turns your logging pipeline into a second, less-protected copy of your most sensitive data. Never write these to a log, even temporarily:

- **Passwords** — not even the failed attempt. A misconfigured log aggregator with broad read access instantly becomes a password-harvesting tool.
- **Session tokens and API keys** — a leaked token in a log is as good as a stolen credential, and logs are typically retained (and searched, and exported) far longer than a session should live.
- **Full card numbers** — PCI-DSS explicitly prohibits logging the full PAN; log a masked form (`**** **** **** 1234`) if you need any reference at all.
- **Unmasked PII** beyond what the investigation genuinely needs — full SSNs, full addresses, health data.

The practical rule: log *that* an authentication attempt happened and whether it succeeded, never the credential itself. If you need to correlate a user's actions, log a stable user ID, not their raw personal data.

slides.sectionTitle: A misconfigured stack as an attack surface map
slides.markdown:
![A three-tier stack with misconfiguration flags at each layer, forming an attacker path from the internet to the database with no code exploit](assets/misconfig-attack-path.svg)

The point the diagram makes visually: none of these three flags is a code vulnerability. An attacker doesn't write an exploit — they run a port scanner, find the open management port, try `admin/admin`, and read the stack trace that told them which ORM and version to look up known issues for. The entire chain is configuration, and the entire chain is fixable without touching application code.

slides.sectionTitle: Enough logging vs logging as a liability
slides.markdown:
| | Enough to detect abuse | Logging that becomes a liability |
|---|---|---|
| **Content** | Event type, user ID, IP, timestamp, outcome | Raw request/response bodies including secrets and PII |
| **Retention** | Set by a policy tied to detection and compliance needs | "Keep everything forever, just in case" |
| **Access** | Restricted to the security/on-call team, audited | Anyone with dashboard access can query it |
| **Alerting** | Thresholds trigger a human or automated response | Logs are written but nobody is watching |
| **Consequence of a breach** | Attacker gains what they already had | Attacker gains a searchable archive of secrets and PII |

The irony worth stating out loud: over-logging in the name of security can hand a breach *more* to steal than under-logging would have. The goal is enough signal to detect and investigate, not a total capture of every byte that ever crossed the wire.

slides.sectionTitle: "Just for debugging, I'll remove it later"
slides.markdown:
The specific trap that catches experienced engineers, not just juniors: adding a temporary `console.log(password)` or logging a full request object "just to debug this one issue in staging," fully intending to remove it before merging.

Why it keeps happening anyway:

- The debug line ships because the fix looked urgent and the removal step got skipped under time pressure.
- Staging and production often share a log aggregator, so a "staging-only" debug line reaches the same retained, searchable index as real customer data.
- Once merged, nobody re-reviews old commits for stray debug logging — it surfaces only in a security audit, months later, if at all.

The fix isn't discipline, it's structural: strip sensitive fields at the logging *library* layer (a redaction filter on known field names like `password`, `token`, `ssn`) so a developer's momentary lapse can't leak a secret even when it happens.

slides.sectionTitle: Hardening as a repeatable process, not a one-off
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
A junior fix for misconfiguration is a one-time hardening pass before launch. A senior fix treats configuration as something that **drifts**, and builds a process that catches drift continuously:

- **Infrastructure as code with a security baseline.** If your cloud resources are defined in Terraform or similar, a misconfigured default (a public storage bucket) is a diffable, reviewable line, not a console click nobody remembers making.
- **Automated configuration scanning** in CI — tools that flag a newly-public S3 bucket, an open security group, or a debug flag left true, before it ships rather than after a scanner finds it in production.
- **Golden images and templates** so every new service starts from a hardened baseline instead of a blank default that someone has to remember to lock down.

The underlying insight: misconfiguration isn't a one-time mistake, it's an ongoing entropy problem. Every new engineer, every new service, every quick fix under deadline pressure is a chance to drift back toward an insecure default — so the defense has to be continuous, not a checklist run once before launch.

slides.sectionTitle: Detection as the last line of defense
slides.markdown:
Logging and monitoring don't prevent a breach — they determine how long one lasts once prevention fails. That reframing matters for how you prioritize:

- **Mean time to detect (MTTD)** is the metric that logging failures actually harm. An attacker with unnoticed access for six months can exfiltrate incrementally, in a pattern designed to stay under any single alert's threshold.
- **Correlation matters more than any single log line.** One failed login is nothing. A thousand failed logins across a thousand different usernames from one IP in ten minutes is a credential-stuffing attack — but only if something is aggregating and comparing, not just storing.
- **Logs need to survive the compromise.** If an attacker who gains admin access can also delete the logs of their own access, you have no forensic trail at all. Ship logs to a separate, write-restricted destination.

Treat logging as your last line of defense, not your first — which means it has to work even when every earlier line already failed.

Misconfiguration and logging failures are the backdrop against which every other topic in this group operates: an [injection attack](injection-attacks) or an [XSS payload](xss) still needs to get through, but a verbose error page or an open admin panel can hand an attacker the reconnaissance they need to skip straight to a working exploit. And when one does land, logging failures are the reason it's discovered in a breach disclosure instead of an alert.

Next up: [Injection Attacks](injection-attacks), the first of the exploit-technique categories, where the failure is a specific payload rather than an absent control.
